newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Haider hails Euro-poll result, chancellor glum.
newsitem.headline: Haider hails Euro-poll result, chancellor glum.

text.p: Austria's triumphant far-right leader Joerg Haider, whose party scored its biggest nationwide result in a European parliament poll on Sunday, said the government faced its Waterloo at the next general election.
"This great result is an historic step for us," Haider said in a first reaction to his Freedom Party's 28 percent poll in the nation's first European elections.

"We've won a lot of support from critics in the population who simply don't agree with the way European integration is progressing," he said. "If the government doesn't change its policies it will meet its Waterloo at the next election."
Austria's next general election must be called by December 1999.
In the Euro-election campaign, Haider spoke out against the Maastricht treaty on closer European political and monetary integration and opposed any move towards a single currency.
A glum Chancellor Franz Vranitkzy, whose Social Democrats slumped to their worst result since Austria adopted democracy in 1918, said the result was clearly no reason to celebrate.

He blamed the Social Democrats' 29.3 percent result, according to computer projections, on a low voter turnout, dismissing suggestions his coalition with the conservative People's Party should change policy course.
"This is a clear defeat," the chancellor told Austrian television. "But I do not see this result as a call by the electorate to change the composition of the government."
But he acknowledged that voters had sent a protest over the introduction in March of a two-year austerity budget, designed to put Austria on course for Europe's planned single currency.
"I will not change the policies I believe are correct," he said. "Joining the EU was the right decision."

Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel of the People's Party, who forced a snap general election last year over budget worries, said his party's 29.5 percent result was its best showing in more than 30 years.
"Our result had everything to do with our clear pro-Europe minded course, the right candidates and a good campaign," Schuessel said.
